issues.legal_issue: A partial partition of property that is capable of physical division is not recognized for income-tax purposes unless the property itself is physically divided.
material_facts: In an income-tax assessment, the family claimed an oral partial partition of eighteen immovable properties among its members.
The members received proportionate undivided shares in each property and separately accounted for and divided the income, but the properties were not physically divided.
The evidence supported the finding that the properties could be apportioned into lots on an equitable basis, with cash payments if needed to equalize the shares, without impairing their utility.
The family did not seriously attempt physical division; it relied on arbitration awards and evidence stating that individual properties could not be divided into ten shares.
issues.conclusion: The properties admitted of physical division, and the claimed arrangement did not satisfy the statutory definition of partition. Mere allocation of undivided shares or division of income was insufficient, so the claim of partial partition was correctly rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 171 and Explanation (a)(i) to the Income-tax Act, 1961, where property admits of physical division, the property must be physically divided; dividing only its income is not partition. Where there are multiple properties, equitable apportionment among the members may constitute physical division, including equalization by cash payments. Hindu law may recognize partition without physical division, as described in Appovier v. Rama Subba Aiyan, but the tax statute imposes additional conditions. Charandas Haridas v. Commissioner of Income-tax was distinguishable because physical division of the relevant managing-agency rights would have required dissolution and reconstitution of firms, and the family had taken the fullest measure possible to divide its interest.

rule.if: tax_assessment_partition_claim and multiple_assets and physical_apportionment_feasible and only_undivided_shares_allocated and no_serious_physical_division_attempt

predicates.tax_assessment_partition_claim: A family previously assessed as undivided claims a partial partition in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.multiple_assets: The claimed partition concerns multiple income-producing assets.
predicates.physical_apportionment_feasible: The assets can be physically apportioned among the members, including through equitable allocation and any needed equalization payments.
predicates.only_undivided_shares_allocated: The members are allocated undivided shares or income rather than physically apportioned property.
predicates.no_serious_physical_division_attempt: The family does not seriously attempt physical apportionment and relies instead on evidence or arrangements for holding undivided shares.

issues.definition: When a family claims a partial partition in an income-tax assessment, and its multiple assets can be physically apportioned but it allocates only undivided shares without seriously attempting that apportionment, the claimed partition is not recognized for tax purposes.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory rule deeming a previously assessed Hindu undivided family to continue applies to a partial partition of property even when the family members remain unchanged.
material_facts: The family had previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
It claimed that some properties had been partitioned while the same members continued to hold the remaining family properties as an undivided family.
The claimed partition was not recognized under the statutory requirements because the properties capable of physical division were not physically divided.
issues.conclusion: The continuation rule applies to a partial partition of property even though the family remains undivided as to its other property and its membership does not change.
issues.legal_principle: Section 171(1), read with the provisions governing claims of total or partial partition and Explanation (b), applies to partial partitions as to property as well as to partitions as to persons. Parliament expressly extended the statutory scheme beyond Section 25A of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, which had not applied to partial partitions. The principle in Appovier v. Rama Subba Aiyan recognizes that property subject to a partial partition may be held by members as tenants-in-common while other family property remains undivided; Section 171 nevertheless supplies a tax-law rule deeming the family to continue until the required finding is recorded. The earlier interpretation in Sir Sunder Singh Majithia v. Commissioner of Income-tax concerned the former statutory scheme.

rule.if: tax_assessment_partition_claim and previously_assessed_family and partial_property_separation and family_membership_unchanged

predicates.tax_assessment_partition_claim: A family previously assessed as undivided asserts a partition during an income-tax assessment.
predicates.previously_assessed_family: The family has previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.partial_property_separation: The family members claim to have separated some property while retaining other property jointly.
predicates.family_membership_unchanged: The same members remain in the family after the claimed separation of property.

issues.definition: If a previously assessed family claims in an income-tax assessment to have separated some property while retaining other property, the statutory continuity rule applies even if its membership remains unchanged.

issues.legal_issue: Income from property subject to a claimed partial partition remains includible in the Hindu undivided family's income unless the required statutory finding of partition is recorded.
material_facts: The family claimed that its properties had been partially partitioned under Hindu law and that income from them thereafter belonged to individual members.
The tax authority rejected the claim because the properties capable of physical division had not been physically divided, and no statutory finding recognizing the partial partition was recorded.
The High Court nevertheless held that the income from those properties should be excluded from the family's income; the Revenue challenged that ruling.
issues.conclusion: The income from the properties remained includible in the family's total income because no finding recognizing the partial partition had been recorded under Section 171.
issues.legal_principle: Section 171(1) deems a family previously assessed as undivided to continue as such except to the extent a finding of partition is given under that section. Under Sections 171(2) and (3), the assessing officer must inquire into the claim and record a finding; the assessment consequences of a qualifying finding are addressed in Sections 171(4) and (5). The definition in the Explanation requires physical division where property admits of it. Section 10(2) does not displace that statutory scheme. The rule differs from the former Section 25A scheme, which did not cover partial partitions. Nor does the analogy to an alienation in favour of a stranger apply where the family seeks to treat its own property as partitioned without satisfying the statutory conditions; A. Kannan Chetty v. Commissioner of Income-tax distinguished an alienation from a family transaction in which the family retains the property and its income.

rule.if: tax_assessment_partition_claim and family_previously_assessed_as_undivided and partition_finding_not_recorded and income_from_claimed_partition_property

predicates.tax_assessment_partition_claim: A family previously assessed as undivided claims a partition in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.family_previously_assessed_as_undivided: The family was previously assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.partition_finding_not_recorded: No statutory finding recognizing the claimed partition has been recorded after inquiry.
predicates.income_from_claimed_partition_property: The income being assessed comes from property that the family claims to have partitioned.

issues.definition: When a previously assessed family claims partition in an income-tax assessment but no statutory finding recognizes it, income from the claimed partition property remains included in the family's total income.
